title: Zechariah 6:1–8
context: Zechariah sees his last night vision: four chariots with red, black, white, and dappled horses come out from between two bronze mountains. The angel who talks with him explains that they are the four winds of the sky going out from the Lord of all the earth; some go north and some south, and the strong horses patrol the earth. The vision ends with the word that those going north have quieted the LORD’s spirit in the north country. The symbolism of the colors, directions, and mountains is held cautiously, and the vision is best read alongside the horsemen of 1:8–11.

verses.text: Again I lifted up my eyes, and saw, and behold, four chariots came out from between two mountains; and the mountains were mountains of bronze.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zechariah sees four chariots coming out from between two mountains of bronze. This is the last of the night visions that began in 1:8.

Arminian readers see God’s rule over the whole earth pictured as active and watchful.
verses.reformedNotes:
The mountains may suggest the entrance to God’s presence, and bronze strength or permanence, though the symbolism is debated.

Reformed readers see God’s sovereign government of history. Shared ground: the vision assures the returned community that God rules.

verses.text: In the first chariot were red horses. In the second chariot were black horses.
verses.arminianNotes:
The first chariot has red horses, the second black horses. The colors are named one by one.

Arminian readers see a vivid picture of God’s agents sent out into the world, without pressing each color for a separate meaning.
verses.reformedNotes:
Some readers connect the colors with judgment, death, or victory; others see them chiefly as distinguishing the teams. Compare the horses of 1:8.

Reformed readers hold the symbolism loosely too. Shared ground: the colors point to God’s varied agents.

verses.text: In the third chariot were white horses. In the fourth chariot were dappled horses, all of them powerful.
verses.arminianNotes:
The third chariot has white horses and the fourth dappled horses, all powerful. The description is complete.

Arminian readers see strength in God’s servants, who go where he sends them.
verses.reformedNotes:
The word “powerful” may describe all the teams or especially the last; readers differ, as they do over the colors.

Reformed readers see the might of God’s instruments. Shared ground: both traditions read the vision as a picture of God’s strong agents.

verses.text: Then I asked the angel who talked with me, “What are these, my lord?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Zechariah asks the angel who talks with him, “What are these, my lord?” The interpreting angel appears again.

Arminian readers see revelation given in response to the prophet’s honest question.
verses.reformedNotes:
The same angel guides Zechariah through the earlier visions (compare 1:9 and 4:4–5).

Reformed readers see God granting understanding through his appointed messenger. Shared ground: both traditions read the question as the normal pattern of these visions, where meaning is explained rather than left to guesswork.

verses.text: The angel answered me, “These are the four winds of the sky, which go out from standing before the Lord of all the earth.
verses.arminianNotes:
The angel answers, “These are the four winds of the sky, which go out from standing before the Lord of all the earth.” The chariots serve God.

Arminian readers see God’s reach to every direction.
verses.reformedNotes:
The four winds may picture the whole earth; compare 2:6, where the LORD scattered his people “as the four winds of the sky.”

Reformed readers see God sending his agents from his presence. Shared ground: God is Lord of all the earth.

verses.text: The one with the black horses goes out toward the north country; and the white went out after them; and the dappled went out toward the south country.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The angel says the black horses go north, the white after them, and the dappled south. The directions are named.

Arminian readers see attention drawn to the north, where the exiles had been.
verses.reformedNotes:
The red horses are not mentioned here, and the direction of the white is uncertain; readers offer various explanations.

Reformed readers see God’s rule over every region. Shared ground: both traditions hold the details loosely and focus on God’s purpose toward the north.

verses.text: The strong went out, and sought to go that they might walk back and forth through the earth. He said, “Go around and through the earth!” So they walked back and forth through the earth.
verses.arminianNotes:
The strong horses seek to go through the earth, and he tells them, “Go around and through the earth!” They patrol the earth.

Arminian readers see God’s watchful oversight extending everywhere.
verses.reformedNotes:
The patrol recalls 1:10–11, where horsemen go “back and forth through the earth.” Who gives the command, the angel or the LORD, is not certain.

Reformed readers see God directing his agents. Shared ground: God watches over the whole world.

verses.text: Then he called to me, and spoke to me, saying, “Behold, those who go toward the north country have quieted my spirit in the north country.”
verses.arminianNotes:
He tells Zechariah that those going north “have quieted my spirit in the north country.” The vision ends with rest.

Arminian readers see God’s purposes accomplished in the north.
verses.reformedNotes:
“My spirit” here may mean God’s anger now satisfied, or his Spirit at work among the exiles; readers differ. The north often stands for Babylon in these chapters.

Reformed readers see God’s purpose fulfilled. Shared ground: God brings rest.
